checkpoints: The contract's job is to let any operator or client answer "who leads right now, how healthy is that, and which leadership period is this" without guessing.
Minimum viable status fields include myId (which replica answered), iAmLeader (this replica's role), and currentLeader (so followers know who to route to).
leaseRemainingMs is a required field — how close the leader is to losing the lease, a health signal rather than a bare boolean.
term is a required field — the monotonic counter that increments on each acquisition.

Defending term is the discriminator between a junior and a senior answer: it distinguishes "old leader, term 1" from "new leader, term 2" even when the same node reclaims leadership twice, making failovers observable in logs and clients.
term is also the seed of a fencing token, since an op can carry term and let a lower tier reject a stale term.
The core invariant the contract must uphold: exactly one replica ever reports iAmLeader=true, and every follower's currentLeader points at that id.

Keep the write side minimal and safe — acquire via SET NX PX, renew via an atomic CAS — and expose state to read without offering any "become leader" override that would let a caller manufacture split brain.
Build the queue entirely on etcd's primitives so the client never computes ordering.
Join is a lease-attached PUT of a uuid-suffixed key under a shared queue prefix; the uuid guarantees no two clients overwrite each other even at the same instant.
The join returns ticketKey, createRevision (read from the PUT response header, never computed), position, and isMyTurn.

createRevision is the ordering primitive: etcd assigns it as it serializes the write through the Raft leader, so two concurrent joins receive different revisions — the race is removed at the consensus layer, not with a client-side lock.

Queue-state asks etcd to sort by Create Ascend, so the head is always the smallest createRevision at index 0 and isMyTurn is just position == 0, with no client-side sort or race window between two reads.

Self-cleaning falls out of the lease: attaching a TTL lease means a dead client's key auto-deletes when its lease expires, so the head can leave without anyone deleting it and everyone shifts up by one.
This is ephemeral-sequential semantics, the etcd equivalent of a ZooKeeper sequential znode.
The invariants to defend: order is imposed by Raft and identical for all observers, and each client must keep-alive faster than the TTL or its ticket expires out from under it.
The naive answer — a flag in a config file — fails: if the flag-holder crashes the job never fires again, and someone has to flip the flag by hand, which is racy.
During that flag-flipping window, two pods can both believe they're the runner.
The real requirement is a self-healing election, not a static marker.
Use a lease: a lock with a built-in TTL, held in one shared store (Redis or etcd).
Every replica ticks; a follower tries SET leader_key myId PX 3000 NX, and NX means exactly one of them wins — that replica becomes leader and is the one that runs the nightly job.
While it's alive, the leader renews the lease before it expires — a heartbeat, not a one-time claim.

When the leader crashes, it simply stops renewing; the lease expires on its own once the TTL elapses, and a follower's SET NX PX now succeeds and takes over — no operator, no manual flag, nothing to page for.
The leaderless gap is bounded, not open-ended: leaseTTL + renewInterval, so with a 3000ms lease and a 1000ms renew tick the worst case is around 4 seconds.
A fencing token only provides real safety if the storage side actually compares it against a watermark.
Object stores, third-party APIs, and event sinks usually don't check anything — they accept whatever write arrives.
A paused client with a stale token can still overwrite fresher data, so the token achieves nothing in that case.
Option 1: wrap the sink behind a service you control that holds the watermark and rejects any token <= lastSeen, forwarding only accepted writes downstream.
That wrapping approach restores real safety but adds an extra hop and a stateful, monotonic watermark that must itself survive restarts.
Option 2: if you genuinely can't wrap the sink, fall back to short TTLs and accept only best-effort safety.
A short lease shrinks the pause-past-TTL window where a stale write can slip through, but does not close it.

Load-bearing principle: never assume every sink understands fencing — the token is only as strong as the layer that checks it, so you either move the check to a layer you control or consciously accept a bounded, best-effort risk.
The worst-case failover window is bounded by leaseTTL + renewInterval — the time for the dead lease to expire plus the time for a follower to detect and grab it.
Setting leaseMs=200 and renewIntervalMs=100 looks tempting because it makes failover near-instant (~300ms).
Below roughly 1-2 seconds, transient network blips and GC pauses routinely make a perfectly-alive leader miss a renewal in time.
That missed renewal makes the lease expire and a follower take over, producing a false step-down (unnecessary failover) more often than a real crash occurs.
Shorter renewal intervals also multiply Redis traffic, since every leader renews more often per second.
The stabilizing rule is to renew at least three times per lease: renewInterval <= leaseMs / 3, so one missed renewal doesn't expire the lease.
With leaseMs=3000 that means renewing every <=1000ms, and production leaves more margin (e.g. 800ms).
Ultimately you tune to the blast radius: an idempotent job tolerates loose, cheap timing, while data corruption risk demands generous margin plus a fencing token/term or a move to consensus.
A Redis lease-based election gives good-enough mutual exclusion with cheap setup and low latency.
Its safety rests on clocks and the assumption that a process never pauses longer than its lease.
A Redis lease is not linearizable and hands you no fencing token for free — you attach the term/token yourself.
Consensus systems (etcd/ZooKeeper) elect through a Raft/Zab quorum, making leadership a majority decision.
Consensus gives linearizable reads and a built-in monotonic sequencer (etcd's revision, ZooKeeper's zxid) usable directly as a fencing token.
Consensus preserves safety even when a node pauses, because the old leader's operation is rejected by quorum.
The cost of consensus is real: extra latency per commit and the operational weight of running an odd-sized cluster.

The decision is governed by the blast radius of being wrong, not by which option is "safer in the abstract": an idempotent duplicated job makes the Redis lease enough and cheap, while data corruption or strict-ordering needs justify paying for consensus — pragmatically start with a lease plus fencing token and escalate to etcd/ZooKeeper only when correctness truly demands linearizability.
Quorum only means anything if the voters can fail independently.
Redlock counts a majority of yes-votes across N nodes so that no single failure can flip the outcome, requiring nodes uncorrelated in network, power, and availability zone.
A Redis Cluster breaks that independence assumption because it replicates between master and replica, so the "nodes" are copies of each other, not independent voters.
During a network partition, a master and a newly promoted replica can both accept SET NX on the same key.
That produces a false quorum that grants the lock to two clients at once — the split-brain the whole design exists to prevent.
Redlock deliberately uses N independent instances (3 in the demo, where majority is 2) with no replication between them, each casting one genuine vote.
Antirez recommends 5 nodes across 5 machines/AZs in production so the deployment tolerates real failures without those failures being correlated.
Letting replication correlate the votes makes the majority count a lie, and liveness collapses into two owners each believing they hold the lock.

In the leader/renew branch, calling `pexpire` on the lease key every tick without first confirming the key's stored value still matches this node's own id extends whatever lease currently occupies that key, regardless of which replica actually owns it.
A replica's local `isLeader` boolean is never re-verified against Redis during renew, so once the underlying key changes ownership the flag can go stale and stop reflecting reality.

If a network blip or slow tick makes a node miss its renewal window, its lease expires and a follower's `SET leader_key myId PX <ttl> NX` legitimately claims the key — yet the demoted node's next tick still calls `pexpire` on that same key, extending a TTL that now belongs to the new leader.
The result is split brain: two replicas both hold `isLeader === true` at the same time and both execute the leader-only job concurrently, even though only one of them actually owns the Redis key.

This failure mode never surfaces under a single-leader smoke test or normal operation, because on the happy path renew always lands before expiry and the key's value never changes underneath the current leader — it only appears after an actual lease-expiry event such as a blip or GC pause.

The correct renew operation is an atomic compare-and-swap executed server-side, e.g. a Lua script that runs `GET` on the key, compares it against this node's own id, and only calls `PEXPIRE` when they match, returning a sentinel value (such as 0) on mismatch.

Redis executes Lua scripts single-threaded, so folding the ownership check and the TTL extension into one script closes the race window that exists when `GET` and `PEXPIRE` are issued as two separate client round-trips.

When the compare-and-swap script reports a mismatch, the node must immediately set `isLeader = false` and log its step-down instead of retrying the renew, falling back to competing for the key via `SET ... NX` like any other follower.

A distributed lock's usable window is not the raw `ttlMs` passed in — it is `ttl − elapsed − drift`, where `elapsed` is however long the acquisition itself took and `drift` compensates for clock skew between the independent Redis nodes voting on the lock.

Because `Promise.all` over the per-node `SET NX PX` calls has no per-node timeout, a single slow or dead node can stretch the real acquisition time close to the full `ttlMs` before the quorum resolves — so `elapsed` can end up nearly as large as `ttl` itself.

Hard-coding `validityMs: ttlMs` in the return value — instead of computing it from `Date.now()` captured before the parallel `SET` calls and subtracted afterward — means the reported validity is completely disconnected from how much of that window the acquisition itself already consumed.

The grant condition should be `acquiredOn >= quorum && validityMs > 0`, not just `acquiredOn >= quorum`; when the computed validity is zero or negative the function must fail closed — releasing the lock on every node and returning `acquired: false` — exactly like the existing failure branch already does for a missed quorum.

The bug is silent on the happy path because when all nodes are healthy, `Promise.all` resolves almost instantly, so real elapsed time is tiny and even a correct calculation would land close to `ttlMs` — meaning the missing `elapsed`/`drift` subtraction never visibly changes the result under normal conditions.

With `ttl=5000ms` and one node taking roughly 4800ms to respond, the real remaining validity is only about 200ms minus drift, yet the unfixed function still reports `validityMs: 5000` and `acquired: true` — so a worker believes it holds the lock for nearly five more seconds when it is already almost expired, letting a second worker acquire the same resource and both believe they hold a valid lock simultaneously (the exact split-brain scenario Redlock's quorum mechanism exists to prevent).

Fixing the acquisition path alone is not sufficient — the `ioredis` client should also have `commandTimeout` (and `connectTimeout`) configured to well under roughly 10% of `ttlMs`, so a single dead node is bounded and cannot drag the whole `Promise.all` call out toward the full `ttl` the way it does in the unbounded version.

Even after correctly computing `validityMs`, the critical section protected by the lock should still finish comfortably inside that window — typical guidance is using no more than about 30% of it — since a shrunk validity is not license to consume every remaining millisecond, leaving margin for release and any residual jitter.

etcd assigns a Raft-ordered `createRevision` to a key at the moment it is written, and that value is already returned in the PUT response header (`putRes.header.revision`) rather than needing to be computed by the client.

Stamping a queue position with `Date.now()` on the client makes ordering depend on wall-clock time, and clocks on different machines can drift, so concurrent joins can leave two clients each believing they hold the head position.
`modRevision` (etcd3's `kv.mod_revision`) changes every time a key's value is written, while `createRevision` is fixed at the moment the key is first created and never changes afterward.

Sorting a queue by `modRevision` instead of `createRevision` causes the queue order to silently reshuffle whenever any ticket's value is updated, even though the ticket's actual join order never changed.

etcd supports server-side ordered retrieval — `getAll().prefix(prefix).sort("Create", "Ascend")` — which returns entries already sorted by creation order and removes the need for the client to compute or re-sort ordering itself.

A single-client demo has no concurrency and no mid-queue updates, so both the wall-clock-position bug and the modRevision-sort bug pass local testing while still being production-breaking under real concurrent load.

Client-computed ordering undermines the core reason to build a queue on etcd in the first place: etcd's Raft consensus already provides a total order across writes, so recomputing that order client-side reintroduces the exact race the system exists to remove.

A correct implementation keeps ticket ordering pinned to `createRevision` even when a ticket's value later changes, such as a progress field being updated mid-queue, since `createRevision` is immutable while `modRevision` moves with every subsequent write to that key.
